transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-01 16:00 PDT — Duration 52m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Oliver (CTO, BrightLane), Priya (Lead Eng), Evan (Product), Sara (Security)

Summary: quick hosted API demo showing chat and text generation basics. Emphasis on streaming, params, and rescue/retry patterns plus where Console helps with Optimize suggestions.

[00:00] Maya: All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer. Uh, we'll run a quick 40-ish minute demo and save time for Q&A. Does that still work for everybody?
[00:12] Oliver: Yep that's good. We have about 45 minutes, trying to get a feel for latency for our route planer microservice.
[00:20] Priya: Also want to make sure how we do retries — we have strict idempotency requirements.
[00:26] Maya: Perfect, we'll cover retries and idempotency patterns. Liam will show live streaming and we'll also pop into the Console Optimize suggestions.
[00:34] Liam: Cool, starting with the hosted chat endpoint — same REST call you all saw in the quickstart. I'm going to kick off a streaming call and you should see partial tokens come over as they generate.
[00:44] Liam: (demoing) Here you can see we set parameters: max_tokens 256, temperature 0.0 for deterministic route summarization, top_p 0.8 for safety, and we wired in a system prompt — in our demo it's 'You are Redwood Route Assist, summarize steps concisely.'
[01:05] Oliver: Quick question — if we have a dropped connection mid-stream, what's the recommended approach?
[01:12] Liam: Great question. We recommend idempotent request IDs plus the resume token pattern. Effectively you can either retry with the same conversation state, or request a continuation from the last token index. For the hosted API we provide a "resume" cursor in the SDK; if you re-open the stream with the same conversation and cursor the model will continue, avoiding duplicate outputs most of the time.
[01:40] Priya: Does that rely on Redwood keeping KV cache state server-side? We're trying to minimize persisted context for compliance.
[01:48] Liam: By default the hosted path keeps ephemeral KV cache for active conversations to speed up responses, but you can also set short TTLs or disable server-side cache and send prefixes from the client. On Dedicated or Private we can give you options to control cache retention and even put logs into your own storage via the VPC connector.
[02:10] Evan: How visible is that in the Console? Can we see token counts per call and the cache hit rate?
[02:18] Maya: Yes, Console breaks down token-level cost, latency, and a cache hit/miss metric per route. Optimize will then suggest batching or quant profiles based on your workload.
[02:30] Liam: I'm going to intentionally throttle the network a bit to show partial chunking and how clients should interpret partial events.
[03:00] Liam: (demo) You can see partial chunks -- sometimes you'll get small fragments that look like '—ing' or incomplete words. Clients should render progressively and handle reflows.
[03:22] Oliver: We saw some garbled proper nouns in a previous PoC — like our depot 'Harrin' was transcribed as 'haring' — is that model-side or the transcription layer?
[03:31] Liam: Likely model tokenization; also if your system prompt doesn't include relevant entity lists the model may normalize names. You can pin with few-shot examples or prompt engineering to keep domain names stable.
[03:50] Priya: On retries, are there backoff recommendations? We can't just hammer the service.
[03:56] Liam: Exponential backoff with jitter is standard. For idempotent generation calls we recommend a short initial backoff (200-500ms) increasing up to a few seconds depending on SLA. Also, handle HTTP 429s by deferring or using our queueing/burst policies — Hosted supports per-tenant burst windows that can be tuned.
[04:20] Maya: Important note: for deterministic results we suggest temperature 0.0 and to pin max tokens, also use best-effort deduping on client side in case of resumed streams.
[04:34] Evan: Can you show how Console surfaces Optimize suggestions for batching? We have a lot of small requests during peak hours.
[04:40] Liam: Sure — switching to Console. Here Optimize shows a histogram of sequence lengths. Based on your distribution, it suggests a batching window and target batch size. If you enable automatic batching on Dedicated you can get 20-40% token cost savings with minimal latency impact for typical logistics uses.
[05:10] Priya: Are these suggestions safe with respect to latency P95? We care about tail latency.
[05:16] Liam: Yeah Optimize gives expected latency delta and an estimated token cost reduction. You can set a latency SLO and Optimize will filter suggestions that breach it.
[05:28] Oliver: What about quantization? We run some smaller models on the edge. Does Redwood recommend certain quant profiles?
[05:36] Liam: We recommend per-workload quant profiles. Console has recommended profiles: 4-bit for throughput-oriented tasks where slight quality loss is acceptable, and 8-bit or none for high-fidelity generation. We'll run a quantization benchmark for your sample prompts to show quality impact.
[05:58] Evan: Security — we need SSO, KMS integration, and SOC2 evidence. Can you cover private deployment options?
[06:06] Maya: Absolutely. For regulated data we offer Private deployment (VPC or on-prem). Private includes customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM, SAML SSO, RBAC, and detailed audit logs with retention controls. We'll send the SOC2 report and architecture doc after the call.
[06:26] Sara: How are audit logs filtered? We can't have driver PII leak into high-level dashboards.
[06:32] Liam: Audit logs can be streamed to your storage, and Console supports redaction filters and per-token scrubbers. On Private you can have logs never leave your VPC.
[06:45] Priya: For the pilot, we want to run throughput tests with our real prompts. Do you have a benchmark harness?
[06:52] Liam: Yes, I'll share a harness and a sample perf spreadsheet. It includes warm/cold run sets and ways to sweep temperature and sequence length. We'll run an initial 5k requests set for your workload.
[07:10] Oliver: Cost question — hosted vs dedicated for bursty daily peaks, which is cheaper?
[07:18] Maya: If your peaks are predictable and high volume, Dedicated reserved capacity tends to be more cost-effective. Hosted is easier to start with and supports burst windows, but sustained high throughput usually benefits from reserved capacity. We'll put numbers against your expected qps in the pricing doc.
[07:36] Evan: Any limitations on streaming payload size? We sometimes send 2k token prompts.
[07:42] Liam: Max sequence limits depend on model variant; we can support up to 8k in many of our curated models, and longer on dedicated hardware. For very long prefixes we recommend prefix-KV caching to reduce costs. Note: sometimes KV gets written as K V in older docs, forgive the inconsistency.
[08:05] Maya: Coming back to retries — if you do a network reconnect, the SDK will either reattach to the same stream or give you a resume cursor. We showed the cursor flow earlier; Liam will share code snippets for that.
[08:18] Liam: (shares code) Example: call.chat.stream({ conversation_id: 'xyz', resume_cursor: last_index }) — the SDK handles partial token dedupe.
[08:30] Priya: Suppose we need to avoid storing any logs for certain conversations — is that doable?
[08:36] Liam: Yes, you can set no-persist flags and the system will avoid writing logs to long-term storage. On hosted we'll still have ephemeral traces for active sessions but they are auto-trimmed. For full no-retain we recommend Private.
[08:52] Oliver: We also want to failover if a model or region becomes unhealthy — what's Redwood's fallback story?
[08:58] Maya: Smart routing — you can set routing policies by latency or cost. If a primary model is unhealthy we can failover to a compatible model family. The Console will show model health and automatic fallback triggers.
[09:14] Evan: Can you demo a quick error and the retry flow?
[09:18] Liam: Sure, I'll simulate a transient 500 on the stream. (demo) Client receives error, SDK retries with exponential backoff, reattaches using resume cursor and the output continues.
[09:40] Liam: Note that some regenerated segments may be slightly different if the model state diverged; that's why idempotent IDs and dedupe checks help.
[09:52] Priya: Do you have guidance for deterministic tasks vs creative tasks?
[09:58] Liam: Deterministic: temperature 0, seed fixed if available, and zero-shot vs few-shot patterns. Creative: higher temp, larger max tokens. Console can suggest per-route defaults.
[10:12] Oliver: For our route ingestion we need to preprocess and postprocess — what's the best place to insert safety/filters?
[10:18] Maya: Pre-filter at client side for PII, then send sanitized prompts. Postprocess in your app for final checks. Console's evals let you run golden prompts to detect regressions after model or config changes.
[10:34] Evan: About the evals — can we run continuous evals on a set of prompts and get alerts?
[10:38] Liam: Yes — Optimize supports evals and alerts on quality regressions; you can tie those into rollouts for automatic rollback if a threshold is breached.
[10:52] Priya: A nit — we saw near-duplicate outputs in our field tests. Any advice?
[10:58] Liam: Use small tweak to temperature or top_p; also enforce client-side dedupe and hash of outputs. For high-precision tasks, increase beam width or use deterministic decoders.
[11:12] Maya: We're at about 11 minutes in the demo — I'll jump to Console quick tour and show the Optimize suggestions dashboard.
[11:18] Liam: (console) Here: per-route dashboards, token breakdown, latency P50/P95, and batching recommendations. Also you can pin a canary rollout and specify a fallback model.
[11:40] Oliver: If we do canary on 5% traffic, can we set region-based routing?
[11:46] Liam: Yes, routing rules can target regions, models, or customer tiers. Canary can be restricted to specific user IDs or regions.
[11:56] Evan: For the pilot, we want to limit to the EU region for data residency reasons. How soon can that be provisioned?
[12:02] Maya: If you're on hosted, we can spin up an EU-tenanted environment within a few days depending on capacity; for Private it's a deployment timeline that we'll coordinate with infra. We'll note that as a dependency.
[12:18] Priya: Any lock-in concerns if we later move models on-prem?
[12:22] Liam: We keep APIs consistent across hosted/dedicated/private to minimize lock-in. You can pin model versions and export configs. Data pipelines will need to be migrated but the runtime APIs are similar.
[12:35] Oliver: Competitors claim they have lower tail latencies — how does Redwood measure P95?
[12:40] Maya: We measure token emit latency and end-to-end request latency in Console. For customers we can run joint benchmarks in your environment to validate P95 numbers.
[12:50] Evan: Let's talk about pilot acceptance criteria — what would you recommend?
[12:55] Liam: Suggested: 1) P95 latency under X ms (we'll fill X after benchmark), 2) token cost per request within target budget, 3) no security red flags from audit docs, 4) successful run of 5k sample requests.
[13:10] Priya: We'll aim to share sample prompts tomorrow.
[13:15] Maya: Great. A quick note on streaming failure modes — two common cases: network disconnects and model preemption on shared hardware. For the second, our Smart routing auto-fails to reserved model variants.
[13:30] Liam: Also brief on idempotency keys — include a unique id per logical request; if you retry the same id, server will dedupe generative outputs for a short window.
[13:44] Oliver: For storage of logs — how long are traces kept by default?
[13:48] Liam: Default retention is 30 days on hosted, configurable. We can extend or route logs to your S3 for longer retention.
[14:00] Priya: One more technical — how does batching interact with streaming? If you batch N small requests, do you still get per-client streaming?
[14:08] Liam: Good point. With continuous batching, we aggregate requests and then stream tokens per original request using per-request channels. There's a small added queuing latency but Optimize will show the tradeoff.
[14:26] Evan: Any best practice for small request spikes?
[14:30] Maya: Use client-side smoothing + small buffering so you can take advantage of batching windows, and set burst policies as a safety net.
[14:40] [Pause as Liam pulls up a small sample harness for perf testing]
[15:10] Liam: Running a quick local perf run: warm start vs cold start differences are visible — warm caches cut token emission latency by ~15-25% on our sample.
[15:34] Priya: That's helpful. For our driver chat we need sub-300ms P95 if possible. Any specific model families we should try?
[15:42] Liam: We'll propose a narrow suite — low-latency curated variants and a dedicated small-context model. We'll include per-model P95 estimates in the benchmark.
[15:56] Oliver: Billing — are we billed per-token or per-request?
[16:00] Maya: Per-token for generations/embeddings; there are also reserved capacity contracts for Dedicated with monthly commits. We'll attach sample cost calculations.
[16:12] Evan: Do you offer cost alerts per route?
[16:16] Liam: Yes, Console supports budgets and alerts by route, model, or team.
[16:22] Sara: On the SOC2 doc — can you confirm redaction of customer PII before sharing?
[16:26] Maya: We'll ensure any shared artifact is scrubbed; for full security review we'll use an NDA channel and the private doc store.
[16:36] Priya: One more: does the SDK support graceful shutdowns so our worker processes don't leave partial streams?
[16:40] Liam: Yes, SDK has an abort hook to request a safe termination and retrieve a final cursor; you'll get final tokens and a resume cursor if needed.
[16:52] Evan: All right I think we covered the core. Anything else on streaming params?
[16:56] Liam: Remember: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, presence_penalty — set them per-route and Console can enforce defaults and lock them down. Also use 'stop' tokens to bound responses.
[17:10] Maya: We're going to pause demo momentarily and list next steps.
[17:18] (short pause)
[17:30] Maya: Recap: we'll send pricing + hosted vs dedicated comparison, Liam will share harness and perf spreadsheet, Sara will send security questions and Redwood will return SOC2 and architecture doc. Customer to provide sample prompts and success criteria.
[17:50] Oliver: Sounds good. We'll aim to review by 10/06.
[17:56] Priya: Can we book the pilot kickoff for the week of 10/12?
[18:00] Maya: Noted — we'll follow up with calendar options.
[18:06] Evan: One last live demo snippet — does the SDK automatically dedupe when reattaching?
[18:10] Liam: Yes, the SDK dedupes by request id and cursor; if server can't reconcile it will return a small overlap and a warning tag.
[18:24] [Cross-talk, scheduling notes]
[20:00] Maya: Okay we'll end early and open for any final Qs.
[20:06] Sara: Please make sure the SOC2 doc includes control mappings for Log Redaction.
[20:12] Liam: Will do.
[20:20] Oliver: Thanks, helpful demo.
[20:24] Maya: Thanks everyone. Post-call we'll email the artifacts.

(End of transcript)
